new_statements.rule_in_words: Eastern Canadian Inuktitut (South Baffin data) has no word stress: no contrastive stress, no fixed or rhythmic stress position, no weight-driven prominence; instead each word is demarcated by an HL pitch contour (H near the word beginning, L on the final syllable) with word-final lengthening and lowered f0/intensity at the right edge, and phrases by boundary tones. The authors extend this conclusion to other Inuktitut varieties on the basis of the literature (Labrador: Pigott; Nunavik: Massenet; cross-dialect: Fortescue 1983).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; the study explicitly looked for alternating (secondary-stress) patterns in duration, f0 and intensity and found none.
new_statements.exceptions: Authors note that if edge effects were (mis)read as stress, the dialogue data (final lengthening, penult/final) and single-word data would point to different locations; f0 H is usually on the 1st-2nd syllable but occasionally as late as the penult; Fortescue 1983 (quoted by them) allows 'a limited degree of extra stress.. for discursive contrastive effect in some varieties'. Older impressionistic accounts differ: Bourquin 1891 (Labrador, after Kleinschmidt) puts the main tone on the antepenult with heavy syllables attracting it and secondary tone on first and last syllables; Smith 1975 gives weight-graded degrees of stress; Massenet 1980 places a purely melodic accent by sentence type (penultimate mora declarative, final mora imperative, antepenultimate interrogative).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level claim tested on words inside scripted dialogues and on single-word (citation-form) utterances from Pirurvik learner recordings (2 speakers); prominence-like cues are analysed as right-edge marking of the prosodic word and intonational phrase, i.e. demarcative/phrasal, not lexical.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement rests on acoustic data from South Baffin Inuktitut (Uqqurmiut, Iqaluit-area Pirurvik recordings), a Baffin subdialect of east2534; the authors explicitly extend the conclusion to 'other varieties of Inuktitut'. Corroborating first-hand acoustic statements saved here cover two further east2534 varieties: Labrador Inuttut / Nunatsiavut (Pigott 2013; Rose, Pigott & Wharram 2012) and Nunavik (Inukjuak speakers, Massenet 1980). The only positional 'rule' found is in 19th-c. Bourquin 1891 for Labrador (antepenult Hauptton, copied from Kleinschmidt's Greenlandic grammar), which modern instrumental work does not confirm. Subdialect glottocodes not verified here.

We also did not find clear evidence that a single syllable within each word carried acoustic characteristics marking it as the most prominent, as would be expected of a primary stress. sources.locator: Section 6 'Conclusion', manuscript p. 37 (published chapter pp. 138-177; published page of this passage not seen). Supporting: sec. 2 ms p. 11 'There is broad agreement that Inuit does not have contrastive stress and no minimal pairs have been reported'; abstract ms p. 1.
sources.note: Instrumental study (duration, f0, intensity) of South Baffin Inuktitut words: no contrastive stress in any Inuit variety; no evidence for fixed, rhythmic, bounded/unbounded or quantity-sensitive stress; no single most-prominent syllable; words are demarcated by an HL contour (H near word beginning, L on final syllable) and final lengthening; concludes stress / word-level prominence has no well-defined status in South Baffin Inuktitut and likely all Inuktitut.

sources.note: Einleitung sec. 22-26 'Betonung der Woerter' (pp. 8-10), largely quoting Kleinschmidt's Greenlandic grammar: syllable weight counted (short V=2, long V=4, coda C=+1); 'Der Hauptton sucht auf der drittletzten Silbe zu ruhen', in 2-3-syllable words on the first syllable; a 'Neben- oder Gegenton' on the first and last syllables of longer words; heavier syllables adjacent to the tone position attract the tone; exclamations and question-final words put the tone on the (lengthened) last syllable. Impressionistic 19th-c. account, Labrador.

In Proceedings of the Workshop on Structure and Constituency in the Languages of the Americas 21 (UBCWPL 46), 30-39. Vancouver: UBC. [downloaded via web.archive.org snapshot of lingpapers.sites.olt.ubc.ca]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Intonational analysis of South Baffin dialogues: every orthographic word marked by an HL fall, intonational phrases by an additional boundary L (rarely H); reviews literature that West Greenlandic, Nunavik (Massenet 1980) and Labrador (Pigott 2012) show no stress; no prosodic domain below the word found.

sources.citation: Pigott, Paul E. 2013. Degemination and prosody in Labrador Inuttut: an acoustic study. MA thesis, Memorial University of Newfoundland. xiv+184 pp. hdl:20.500.14783/12913.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Abstract p. ii and ch. 5.3/6 (pp. 107ff, 128-129): Labrador Inuttut 'seems to be devoid of any type of metrical conditioning in any of the standardly-assumed phonetic correlates of stress (intensity, duration or pitch)'; intensity peaks at speaker's discretion; systematic phrase-final lengthening with HL/HLH boundary tones; calls it a 'free or unsystematic stress system', syllable-timed. Reviews Kleinschmidt 1851 and Smith 1975 (three degrees of stress by syllable type) and finds no acoustic support.

sources.citation: Rose, Yvan, Paul Pigott & Douglas Wharram. 2012. Schneider's Law revisited: The syllable-level remnant of an older metrical rule. McGill Working Papers in Linguistics 22(1), 12 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Praat measurements of 17 Labrador consultants: 'intensity peaks can fall on any syllable, except the initial one'; 'stress is in fact at the speaker's discretion.. certainly not as a form of metrical conditioning'; no consistent pitch/duration pattern except phrase-final HLH contours; supports 'Jacobsen's (2000) contention that Inuktitut is not a stress language'.

sources.citation: Massenet, Jean-Marie. 1980. Notes sur l'intonation finale en inuktitut. Cahier de linguistique 10: 195-214. doi:10.7202/800091ar. (speakers from Inukjuak/Port Harrison, Nunavik, recorded at Resolute; instrumental pitch/intensity traces)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: pp. 204-205 (sec. 3-3.1): the 'accent musical' (pitch peak) falls on the last vowel mora in imperatives, the penultimate mora in declaratives, the antepenultimate in interrogatives; intensity traces 'ne presentent aucune structure bien definie. Il semble donc que l'accent d'intensite ne joue aucun role pertinent en inuktitut'; those who report intensity stress have confused it with the sentence-type-dependent musical accent or with consonant tension before geminates; Inuktitut is a mora language.

sources.citation: Beach, Matthew David (2012). Studies in Inuktitut grammar. State University of New York at Buffalo. xiv+410 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online (also online with a university library login)
sources.note: The work says nothing about word-level stress or prominence, so it neither supports nor contradicts the catalog's empty rule or the Arnhold, Elfner & Compton (2023) 'no metrical stress system' statement. Its one intonation remark (sentence-final rise + lengthening on yes/no questions) is compatible with the phrase-level-prosody picture in Arnhold et al. and Massenet 1980 but is not a stress claim. Dialect described is mostly Tarramiutut (Ungava Bay, Nunavik), not the South Baffin variety of the existing statement.
